headings.text: Responsible robotics & AI: a question of ethics?
How to think of robotics, AI & society?
1. Think of robotics & AI as things in the world
2. Robotics & AI are ways of seeing, ordering, intervening
3. Algorithms as recipes for creating new realities
4. Robotics & AI as a vision of a future society

html:
The big picture

The course doesn't ask "is AI good or bad?" and it doesn't treat ethics as solving abstract dilemmas. The lecture contrasts quandary ethics (the trolley problem: choose between options, stripped of context) with a social-science view of AI: AI is not a disembodied intelligence but technical and social practices, institutions, infrastructures, politics and culture (Crawford). Four lenses follow from that: AI as things in the world (made of data, objects and human work), as ways of seeing, ordering and intervening (simplifying complex problems into actionable outputs), as recipes that create new realities (Amoore), and as a vision of a future society that risks solutionism (Morozov). "Responsible" robotics & AI therefore means more than judging finished systems: asking what technologies are and do, how they interact with the social world, and how to design them acceptably and desirably.

Introduction

Opening slides: a still from an AI-generated "Heidi" trailer and a YouTube comment on it: "This is not the Alps. This is the Uncanny Valley." (Link in Online resources below.)

In today's class:

  • a bit about the lecturer and a few questions for you;
  • responsible robotics & AI: a question of ethics?
  • overview of the course;
  • assignments and grading.

About the lecturer: associate professor at the Department of Society, Knowledge and Politics; has worked in Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and the United States; research focus: organisational and material infrastructures for research in the life sciences (human medicine and nature conservation).

Responsible robotics & AI: a question of ethics?

Slides show an image of a robot in a burning city and Raphael's "School of Athens".

A question of ethics?

  • Defining the good life.
  • What to do in a certain situation?
  • Who can be expected to do the right thing?
Intuition

These are three classic questions of ethics: what is worth aiming for (the good life), how to act here and now (the right action), and who carries responsibility (the agent). For AI the third gets hard: when a system acts, is it the developer, the company, the user, or nobody? That question returns in class 10 (Class 10 – Governance and responsibility).

Quandary ethics – the "trolley problem"

  • Abstract definition of ethical problems.
  • Choice between different options without context.
  • What matters about a particular situation in ethical terms?

Cartoon on the slide: a self-driving car at the switch of a trolley track: "Please don't make me choose! Just tell me what to do."

What is the trolley problem, and why is the lecture sceptical of it?

A runaway trolley will kill five people; pulling a lever diverts it onto a track where it kills one. Do you pull it? Versions of it are used to ask how a self-driving car should choose whom to harm in an unavoidable crash. The lecture's point is in the bullets: this quandary ethics strips away context (who built the road, why the brakes failed, who decided to deploy the car, who bears the risk) and reduces ethics to one forced choice at one moment. The course asks the opposite question: what matters about the particular situation, and how did the situation come about?

How to think of robotics, AI & society?

  • AI cannot model human intelligence.
  • Intelligence does not exist in the abstract.
  • It is never independent of material and human resources.

"At a fundamental level, AI is technical and social practices, institutions and infrastructures, politics and culture." — Kate Crawford, Atlas of AI, p. 8

Connection

Crawford's "material" view is exactly the topic of class 4: data centres, energy and critical minerals (Class 04 – Human and environmental costs), and of the hidden human labour (data labelling, content moderation) described there.

1. Think of robotics & AI as things in the world

  • Technologies connected to "real" objects, places, histories.
  • New ways of seeing/doing things, new connections of people and things.
  • E.g. training sets of existing data, requiring human work.

2. Robotics & AI are ways of seeing, ordering, intervening

  • Often requires making complex problems simpler.
  • Moving from attributes to actionable outputs.
  • Involves selection of data considered (not) important.
Worked example — reading a system through lenses 1 and 2

Take an AI that ranks job applicants.

  1. Thing in the world: it is built from past hiring records (data that real recruiters produced), runs on servers, and needed people to label "good hires".
  2. Seeing: it turns a person into attributes (degree, years of experience, keywords).
  3. Ordering: it sorts people into a ranking, i.e. a simplified version of "who is suitable".
  4. Intervening: the output is actionable (invite the top 10), and whatever data were judged unimportant (career breaks, caring work) simply don't count. The ethical questions sit in steps 1–4, long before anyone faces a dramatic "trolley" choice.

3. Algorithms as recipes for creating new realities

"algorithms are generating the bounded conditions of what [things like] a democracy, a border crossing, a social movement, an election, or a public protest could be in the world" — Louise Amoore, Cloud Ethics, p. 4

Intuition

An algorithm doesn't only describe the world, it sets the frame for what can happen in it. If a border system decides who is "risky", then what a border crossing is (for that person) changes; if a feed algorithm decides which posts are visible, it shapes what a protest can become. "Recipe" because it prescribes steps that produce an outcome.

4. Robotics & AI as a vision of a future society

  • "Solutionism": the idea that technology can solve all problems;
  • or: problems worth solving are problems tech can solve.

"Celebrating innovation for its own sake is in bad taste. For technology truly to augment reality, its designers and engineers should get a better idea of the complex practices that our reality is composed of." — Evgeny Morozov, To Save Everything, Click Here, p. 13

Unclear (slide 18)

The slide spells the author "Mozorov"; it's Evgeny Morozov (as on the literature slide).

Common mistake — solutionism

Tempting: "there's a problem, so there must be an app (or a robot, or a model) for it". Solutionism goes wrong in two ways: it redefines problems so that technology can solve them (loneliness → a chatbot), and it ignores problems technology can't touch (why people are lonely). Morozov's fix is not "no technology" but understanding the complex practices a technology lands in first. Compare "innovation for its own sake" with Russell & Vinsel's critique in Class 02 – The bigger picture.

Slide 19 shows headlines on AI extinction risk ("AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?"; "A.I. could possibly end humanity…"; "How would AI actually kill all humans? Here are the top 5 scenarios"). Links in Online resources.

Responsible robotics & AI

  • More than just ethical implications of finished systems.
  • Think more profoundly about what technologies are and do.
  • How do they interact with the social world?
  • How to design in an acceptable and desirable way?
Why "more than ethical implications of finished systems"?

If ethics only starts once a system is built, the important decisions are already made: which problem to solve, which data to use, whom to design for, who carries the risk. Assessing a finished product can at most say "deploy" or "don't". Thinking about what a technology is and does during design lets you change those earlier choices, which is what the group project asks you to do for an imagined system.

Overview of the course

Slides show screenshots of the Moodle course page (syllabus, course readings, lecture slides, group distribution).

  • Twelve class sessions, (almost) every Thursday.
  • Three individual assignments and one group assignment.
  • All information should be in the syllabus (on Moodle), but don't hesitate to ask any questions!

Lecture themes

  1. Introduction & Course Overview (today)
  2. The bigger picture: how technology and society relate (15 Oct)
  3. Datasets & classifications (5 Nov)
  4. Key concerns: human and environmental costs (12 Nov)
  5. Key concerns: bias and discrimination (19 Nov)
  6. Use case I: AI use in education (26 Nov)
  7. Use case II: AI uses in medicine and health care (3 Dec)
  8. Use case III: AI in the arts and creativity (10 Dec)
  9. Use case IV: military uses of AI (17 Dec)
  10. Governance and responsibility (7 Jan)
  11. Regulating robotics and AI (14 Jan)
  12. Creating responsible robotics & AI: course conclusion & evaluation (21 Jan)

Course readings

  • One or two (short) texts about themes related to the lecture.
  • Please read in advance and be prepared to discuss!
  • Texts may explain lecture themes, provide illustrations, or provide food for thought/discussion — they are not "classic" study texts.
Connection

Summaries of all readings: the readings/ folder, starting with Class 02 – The bigger picture.

Assignments and grading

  • Individual assignment 1 (5 Nov): reflection on generative AI — you get a text or an image produced with generative AI and answer three questions given in class.
  • Individual assignment 2 (14 Jan): AI regulation — propose a set of rules to regulate AI and/or robotics applications.
  • Individual assignment 3: mini-tests — four during the semester, of which you must complete three. They assess whether you understood the key themes discussed in class, can be taken at any time during class, and ask about the lectures, the readings, or both.
  • Group assignment: each group presents an (imagined) robotics/AI system and its social & ethical aspects. Groups are distributed at random via Moodle; only in extraordinary cases can they be changed. Laura Schaffer (tutor) can help develop the presentation.

Grading. All assignments must be completed for a positive grade. Each is graded 1 (very good) to 5 (fail), weighted as below; an average better than 4.5 is required to pass.

Assignment% of total
Reflection assignment I25
Reflection assignment II25
Mini-tests (in class)20
Group project30

Literature for the lecture

  • Amoore, Louise (2020): Cloud Ethics. Algorithms and the attributes of ourselves and others. Durham: Duke University Press (esp. Introduction).
  • Crawford, Kate (2021): Atlas of AI. Power, politics, and the planetary costs of artificial intelligence. New Haven: Yale University Press.
  • Morozov, Evgeny (2013): To save everything, click here. Technology, solutionism and the urge to fix problems that don't exist. London: Allen Lane.
